intrinsic_value_estimate: About $62–88 per share (central about $75). Method: owner earnings (brk-letter-1986). 1988 owner earnings were $2.23–2.85/share, midpoint $2.54: net income $1,045M + D&A $170M − equity income not received in cash $36M − capex $387M to ($790M–1,010M), over 354.8M shares. Valued on the basis that the future 'develops much along the lines of its past' (brk-letter-1981#3): 10–15% growth for 10 years, then zero growth, discounted at 9% (pension discount rate used as a proxy for the bond yield) to 12% (management's after-tax cost of capital), plus about $5/share for bottler and CPE stakes. Bounds: no growth $26–33; fading growth at 12% about $46; past continuing at 9% about $88. Net-working-capital (bargain) value is $1.06/share, so the stock fails that test.
margin_of_safety: About 25–47% below intrinsic value at $46.56 in the main cases ($62–88), and about nil only if growth slows to 10% and the discount rate is 12% ($46). The price implies just 3–6% perpetual growth against 13–16% historical per-share growth. There is no asset-based margin: the price is 44x net working capital and 5.4x book. The margin rests on how predictable the franchise is, not on the balance sheet. The framework sets no numeric hurdle at this date for outstanding businesses; the standard is a 'sensible price' (brk-letter-1987#18), and this price meets it.

key_reasons.reason: Not a turnaround and not a business that needs debt; it passes every gatekeeper filter
key_reasons.framework_principle: §2 Filters: turnarounds seldom turn; avoid businesses that need debt (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1982)
key_reasons.evidence: EPS from continuing operations rose every year from $0.79 (1976) to $2.85 (1988). Net debt/net capital 24.3% (ceiling 35%). Capex $387M vs operating cash flow $1,167M in 1988; borrowing paid for buybacks, not operations.

key_reasons.reason: The core business earns exceptional returns without depending on leverage
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE rose from about 20% (1979–83) to 33.3% in 1988. Unlevered return on net capital about 24% after tax. Soft-drink operating income / identifiable assets 44.4% pre-tax in 1988 (international 63.8%).

key_reasons.reason: A wide and widening moat built on brand, scale and distribution, with clear pricing power
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16)
key_reasons.evidence: World soft-drink share rose from <38% (1980) to about 45% (1988), more than double the nearest rival. U.S. fountain 59%. Gross margin 50.5% to 55.6% (1985–88). Concentrate gross margin about 63%. Landor surveys show Coca-Cola 'off the charts'. International consumption per person about 51 servings vs 274 in the U.S.

key_reasons.reason: Strong owner earnings with low capital requirements, so growth does not consume cash
key_reasons.evidence: 1988 owner earnings $790M–1,010M ($2.23–2.85/share). Soft-drink capex $239M vs soft-drink operating income $1,691M. Cash from operations exceeded net income.

key_reasons.reason: Management has created far more than $1 of market value for each $1 retained, and its buybacks were at prices below intrinsic value
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value; buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1983, brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: Per share 1981–88: about $6.46 retained vs a $33.50 price gain (about $5.20 per $1). 69.5M shares repurchased 1984–88 at about $31.5 average; the 1987–88 buybacks at about $40–43 were about one-third below the $62–88 value estimate.

key_reasons.reason: Able, shareholder-oriented management is already in place, and the reporting is candid on the important financial points
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Honest, able management in place; candid reporting (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1983#2)
key_reasons.evidence: Goizueta/Keough since 1981. Stated objective is shareholder value with a 12% cost-of-capital hurdle. Disclosed that current-cost income is lower than reported, flagged inflated volume figures (Australia, U.S. shipments), separated out the $0.35 of 1986 unusual items, and has refocused to >90% soft drinks.

key_reasons.reason: An outstanding business at a sensible price: the market prices in far less growth than the record supports
key_reasons.framework_principle: §5 Valuation, as updated by the investor's later writing (brk-letter-1987#18 'outstanding business at a sensible price'; brk-letter-1981#3 prices that make sense if the past continues)
key_reasons.evidence: Price $46.56 = 16.3x 1988 EPS; owner-earnings yield about 5.5%. The price implies 3–6% perpetual growth vs 13.6–16.1% EPS compounding; the value estimate of $62–88 implies a 25–47% margin.

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed because compounding owner earnings will eventually be reflected in the price
key_reasons.framework_principle: §6 No catalyst needed; Mr. Market is there to serve, not guide (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: Management guides to mid-teens 1989 EPS growth (upi-1989-01-31); dividend raised 13.3%; 14.4M shares remain in the buyback authorization. There is no work-out or control angle.

key_reasons.reason: The facts are clear and the business is very unlikely to change drastically, which justifies concentration, though below the maximum
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear, up to 40% (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: A 100-year franchise with eight years of share gains and rising margins justifies a large position. The size is held to about 25% because the no-growth value (about $33) is below the price, 76% of operating income is foreign, and management has not been met.

risks: Currency: about 76% of operating income is earned outside the U.S.; key currencies rose 27%/16%/10% against the dollar in 1986–88, inflating growth that a stronger dollar would reverse
Growth dependence: the no-growth value ($26–33) is below the price, so a misjudgment of future economics would cause a permanent loss (brk-letter-1981#3 category 2 error)
Capital allocation: bottler stakes (~$1.3B), Foods and the CPE stake earn below management's own 12% hurdle; the 1982–86 entertainment diversification shows a tendency to diversify that could return

Leverage: the self-imposed 35% net debt/capital ceiling and buybacks funded with debt (debt/capital reached 48% in 1987) are more than the framework favors; bottler debt (CCE) sits off the balance sheet
Intense U.S. competition: U.S. soft-drink margins (about 15%) and returns are far below international
Latin American hyperinflation (Brazil and Argentina volume and operating income fell in 1988)
Accounting complexity: three consecutive restatements, gains on sales of subsidiary shares booked in income, a pending FASB 96 charge of about $175M to equity
Compensation tied to the stock price; option grants jumped to 4.18M in 1988
No personal assessment of management, which the framework normally relies on
what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that most of the capital spending is maintenance rather than growth, which would put owner earnings at or below about $2.23 and value near the price
Long-term Treasury yields well above 9–10%, which would compress value toward or below $46
Volume and operating income growth that, once currency effects are stripped out, turns out to be in the low single digits
Competitor data showing Pepsi or others gaining share or forcing price concessions in the U.S. or key international markets
Bottler-system economics showing that Coke must keep supporting over-leveraged bottlers with capital or marketing payments
A meeting with management or a proxy review that reveals poor character, entrenchment, or plans for large diversifying acquisitions
The price running far above the value range before the position is built, which would mean stopping purchases rather than chasing
sell_triggers: Lasting erosion of the moat: world or U.S. share declining for several years, or a sustained fall in gross and concentrate margins indicating lost pricing power

Management deploying large amounts of capital outside the core at sub-hurdle returns (a repeat of the entertainment-style diversification) or issuing stock at prices below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1982#17)
Leverage rising beyond the 35% ceiling to fund non-core uses, making this a business that 'needs debt'
Discovery that the business's economics were fundamentally misread; the position is marketable, so exit is easier than with a controlled company (brk-letter-1987#18)
Loss of confidence in management's integrity or candor; price alone is not a trigger under the permanent-holding default (§8)
